title: Why cutting SaaS prices backfires: raise prices, don't lower them
summary: Rob Walling uses Neil Magnuson's $99 to $19 price cut (LTV fell from $683 to $68) to show that low prices attract price-sensitive, high-churn, high-support customers. He argues most founders underprice from fear, and that raising prices within a segment or moving upmarket yields healthier businesses.

principles.text: Cutting price to grow faster usually makes the whole business worse, as lifetime value collapses more than conversions rise.
principles.quote: Dropping your prices feels like it will instantly improve conversions. Sometimes in the short term, it does. [...] but usually in almost every case I've ever seen in 20 years of doing this, it just makes the whole business worse.

principles.text: Price is a filter: low prices attract kick-the-tires, price-sensitive buyers who churn at the first cheaper alternative.
principles.quote: your price isn't just a number. It's usually a filter. And when you set it too low, you filter in exactly the wrong kind of customers.

principles.text: Higher prices bring committed business buyers who onboard properly, stay longer and need less support.
principles.quote: It provides just enough friction that people can be more committed to trying out your product. These buyers who expect more from you expect more from themselves

principles.text: Most founders underprice out of fear or by anchoring to their costs; the default advice is to charge more.
principles.quote: Most founders anchor their price too low from day one, often out of fear, not out of strategy. They often anchor it to their cost of doing business

principles.text: Founders almost never hit a price ceiling; very few who raise prices end up reversing.
principles.quote: across the literally hundreds and hundreds of companies that I have seen increase their pricing, I believe I know of two, maybe three, that have raised them too high

principles.text: Distinguish raising prices within a segment (test it as an experiment on new customers) from going upmarket (a different customer and sales motion).
principles.quote: Are you raising prices within your current customer segment, or are you trying to move to a different one entirely? Those are two completely different moves.
